en: The Chapter on Non-duality (Advaitaprakaraṇa).

The determination of the syllable *oṃ* has been stated [in the previous chapter] by means of a mere proposition: "The Self is non-dual, auspicious, and the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)."
And it is said: "When [reality] is known, duality does not exist.

In that regard, the non-existence of duality has been established through the section on falsity (*vaitathya-prakaraṇa*) by means of analogies such as dreams, illusions, and cities of the Gandharvas, as well as by reasoning based on grounds such as being an object of perception and having an end. Now, one might ask: is non-duality to be understood through scripture alone, or also by means of reasoning? To this, he says: "It can also be known through reasoning."

How is this so? The section on non-duality (*advaitaprakaraṇa*) is now commenced to establish that the entire collection of distinctions such as the object of meditation and the act of meditation is false, and that the Self alone is non-dual and the ultimate reality, as was concluded in the preceding section. For it is said:
"The dharma based on meditation exists within Brahman only after [the world] has been born;
since everything was unborn prior to its origination, that [meditator] is considered pitiable. (MandU 3.1)

One who relies on meditation—the meditator who has understood meditation as the means to his own liberation, thinking, "I am the worshipper; Brahman is my object of worship"—having performed that meditation, now exists within the manifested Brahman. He thinks: "After the fall of this body, I shall attain the unborn Brahman; and prior to its manifestation, all this and I were the unborn. Whatever was my nature prior to manifestation, now that I am born and exist within the manifested Brahman, through meditation I shall become that very same [Brahman] once again."

The meaning is this: the dharma based on such meditation, thinking "I shall attain [Brahman]," is that by which one becomes a seeker; because of such a meager knowledge of Brahman, he is considered "miserable," "wretched," and "insignificant" by those who constantly perceive the unborn Brahman.
As it is said: "That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed..."
"Know that very Brahman, and not this which they worship here"—such is the Śruti of the Talavakāras (Kena Upaniṣad 1.4). //1//
START MandUpK 3.2:

Being unable to realize the unborn Self which is both external and internal, and considering himself miserable due to ignorance, he thinks, "I am born; I exist within the born Brahman; by resorting to its worship, I shall attain Brahman"—thus he has resolved.
Because one becomes miserable [due to attachment], I shall therefore explain non-miserliness— that which has attained the state of equality and is unborn—
so that nothing whatsoever is born anywhere while it is being born.
Therefore, I shall speak of the unborn Brahman, which is free from the state of wretchedness and miserliness;

for that [Brahman] is not the locus of wretchedness, according to such scriptural passages as: "Where one sees another, hears another, or cognizes another—that is the small, mortal, and unreal" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
The opposite of that is Brahman, called the Infinite (bhūman), which is without inner or outer and free from the wretchedness of birth;
the meaning is: "I shall describe that wretchedness [of birth] by attaining which there is the cessation of all wretchedness produced by ignorance.
That is "unborn" (ajāti); its birth does not exist, it has attained equanimity, having reached total equality.
Why? Because there is no inequality of parts.

For whatever entity possesses parts is said to be "born" when it undergoes an inequality of those parts. But since this [atom] has reached a state of equilibrium due to its partlessness, it does not burst apart by means of any parts; therefore, it is not of inferior quality.

The meaning is: "Listen to that manner by which, on all sides and in every respect, not even the slightest thing is born and nothing bursts forth—just as [the appearance of] a snake in a rope is produced through the vision created by ignorance; in whatever way it is unborn, Brahman remains entirely unborn from every side. //2//
START MandUpK 3.3:
Having promised, "I shall speak of non-birth and the wretchedness of Brahman," he says the following to state the reason and the illustrative example for the sake of establishing that [promise]:
For the Self has arisen as individual souls like space, like the spaces within jars, and like the jars themselves; this is the illustration regarding its manifestation. (MandU 3.3)

Since the Self is indeed other [than the body], subtle like space, partless, and all-pervading—just as space is said to be so—it is declared by the individual souls (jīvas), who are knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas), to be equal to the space within jars, just like the space within jars; thus that supreme Self is equal to space. Alternatively, just as space is said to arise through the spaces within jars, so too does the supreme [Self] arise through the individual souls.

The intention is that the origination of individual selves (jīvātman) from the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is heard in the Vedāntas, is not ultimately real (paramārtha), being comparable to the origination of the space within a jar (ghaṭākāśa) from the great space (mahākāśa).

Just as jars and other composite objects arise from that very space, so too do the aggregates of elements such as earth, as well as internal aggregates characterized by effects and instruments, arise from the Supreme Self— which stands in the place of space— and are conceptually constructed (vikalpita) like a snake [imagined] upon a rope.
Therefore it is said: "And like a jar and so forth, [the Self] has arisen from combinations.

When the Śruti speaks of the birth of the Self, of the individual soul (jīva), and so on, for the sake of instructing those of dull intellect, then, while such birth is being accepted, this illustration—the example beginning with "like the aforementioned space"—is given.
Just as when jars and other such objects have dissolved, the spaces within those jars and so forth merge completely into the [great] space,
even so do the individual souls here merge into the Self.
Just as with the production of a jar or the like there is the production of the "space within the jar" and so forth,

or just as with the dissolution of a jar or the like there is the dissolution of the "space within the jar" and so forth— likewise, with the production of the aggregate of the body and so forth there is the production of the individual soul (jīva), and upon its dissolution, the souls dissolve here into this Self, but not by their own nature; such is the meaning.

Regarding those dualists who assert that if the self were one in all bodies, then when one self experiences birth, death, pleasure, and so forth, all selves would be connected to those states, and there would be a confusion of actions and their fruits—to them this is said: "Just as when the space within one jar is joined with dust, smoke, and the like, not all [spaces] are joined with them; in the same way, the individual souls [are not joined] with pleasure and the like. (MandU 3.5)

Just as when one space within a jar is joined with or affected by dust, smoke, and so forth, all other spaces within jars and the like are not thereby joined with that dust, smoke, and so forth—in the same way, individual souls (*jīva*) are [not affected] by pleasure and the like.
Is it not the case that there is only one Self?
Indeed, it is so. Have you not heard that the Self is one and the same in all aggregates, like space?
If the self were indeed one, then it would follow that it is happy and suffering everywhere;
however, this objection from the Sāṃkhya is not possible,
for the Sāṃkhya does not maintain that the self possesses happiness, suffering, and so forth, since he accepts that happiness, suffering, and the rest are inherent in the intellect (*buddhi*).
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition for the conceptualization of difference within the Self, whose nature is pure perception.
If it is argued that in the absence of such difference, the subservience of the Pradhāna to another purpose would be untenable, we reply:
no, because the purpose accomplished by the Pradhāna does not inhere in the Self.

For if the purpose of bondage or liberation were to inhere in the *puruṣas* by way of distinction from the *pradhāna*, then the *pradhāna*'s subservience to another (its *pārārthya*) would not be possible if the self were one; thus, the postulation of a plurality of *puruṣas* would be logical.
However, the Sāṃkhyas do not accept that bondage or liberation as a purpose inheres in the *puruṣa*;
rather, they maintain that the selves (*ātman*) are consciousness-only and devoid of all distinctions.
Therefore, it is established that the subservience of the *pradhāna* is necessitated solely by the mere existence of the *puruṣa*, and not by the plurality of *puruṣas*.

Consequently, the subservience of the *pradhāna* is not the reason for postulating a plurality of *puruṣas*. Furthermore, the Sāṅkhyas possess no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of a plurality of *puruṣas*.

Pradhāna itself is bound and liberated by taking as its sole cause the mere existence of another (the Puruṣa). And this "other" is the cause for the activity of Pradhāna merely by virtue of having the nature of pure consciousness, without any specific distinction whatsoever. Thus, the postulation of a plurality of Puruṣas and the abandonment of the meaning of the Vedas are due solely to delusion.
As for those such as the Vaiśeṣikas who say that desire and so forth are inherent in the self (ātman), [that too is incorrect].
That too is incorrect;
because the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), which are the causes of memory, do not inhere in a partless self (*ātman*),
and because memory arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātma-manaḥ-saṃyoga*), the restriction of memory is untenable.
Alternatively, there would be the undesirable consequence of all memories arising simultaneously.
Furthermore, it is not logical for selves—which belong to different classes and are devoid of contact and other such qualities—to have a connection with the mind and its faculties.
Nor, according to the opponents, do qualities such as form, nor actions, universals, particulars, or inherence exist as distinct entities from the substance.
For if desire and the rest were absolutely distinct from the substance—the self—then, that being the case, their connection with the substance would be untenable.
If it is argued that a connection characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) is not contradicted for things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*), we say no;
because the eternal self is established prior to the non-eternal desires and so forth, the status of being inseparable is not possible.
If desire and the other qualities were inseparable from the self, it would follow that they are eternal, just like the magnitude residing in the self;
and that is undesirable,
because it would entail the impossibility of liberation for the self.

Furthermore, if inherence (*samavāya*) were distinct from substance (*dravya*), another relation between it and substance would have to be stated, just as there is one between substance and quality (*guṇa*). If it is argued that inherence is itself an eternal relation and thus no further relation need be stated, then it follows that those things possessing the relation of inherence would themselves be eternally related, which renders their separateness impossible.

Moreover, if substances and so forth were absolutely separate, then—just as between a tangible substance and an intangible substance—the sense expressed by the genitive case (the relation of "belonging to") would be untenable.
If the self were a quality subject to the arising and passing away of desire and so forth, it would follow that it is impermanent;
furthermore, like the body, its fruits, and so on, it would possess parts and be subject to modification—just as the body is—and thus these defects would be unavoidable.

However, just as space possesses defects such as being covered by dust, smoke, and impurity which are superimposed upon it through ignorance, so too the self possesses defects such as pleasure and pain caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) like the intellect (buddhi), which are superimposed through ignorance; and thus [concepts such as] bondage and liberation [are possible].
Conventional practices are not contradicted, because all proponents accept that conventional discourse is produced by ignorance and do not accept [the existence of] ultimate reality.
Therefore, the conceptualization of a distinction between selves is performed in vain by the logicians. //5//
START MandUpK 3.6 But how is it that, in the case of a single Self, a conventional usage as if caused by a difference between selves is possible when it is actually produced by ignorance? It is said:
"Indeed, forms, functions, and designations differ here and there."
There is no division in space; such is the determination regarding individual souls.
Just as here, within a single space, the spaces enclosed by a jar, a water-pot, a room, and so forth, differ in form— such as being small, large, and so on—

likewise, their effects, such as the fetching of water, holding [water], or serving as a bed, as well as their designations, such as "the space of the jar" or "the space of the water-pot," are seen to be distinct;
the meaning is that these are differentiated in each respective case as objects of conventional usage.
This entire conventional usage of space as differentiated by form and so forth is not ultimately real;
for in ultimate reality, there is no differentiation of space.
Nor is there any conventional usage based on a differentiation of space except through the gateway of external limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Just as this [is the case], so too, by means of investigation, a determination—that is, a certainty—has been established by the wise regarding the individual selves (jīvas), which are like the space within jars, produced through the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhis). //6//
START MandUpK 3.7:
But is it not the case that in those instances, such as the space within a jar, the conventional usage of distinctions regarding form, function, and so forth, is indeed based on ultimate reality?
This is not so, because:
Just as the space within a jar is neither a modification nor a part of space,
so too the living being (jīva) is never a modification nor a part of the Self (ātman).
The space within a jar is not a modification of the ultimate space, just as a necklace is not a modification of gold, or as foam, bubbles, ice, and so forth are not modifications of water;
nor is it a part, like a branch is of a tree.

Just as the space within a jar is neither a modification nor a part of the [great] ether, so too the individual soul (jīva)—which occupies the place of the space within a jar—is at no time whatsoever a modification or a part of the Supreme Self, which is the ultimate reality and occupies the place of the great ether; it is not so, according to the aforementioned illustration.
Therefore, the meaning is that the worldly transaction based on a distinction between selves is purely illusory. //7//
START MandUpK 3.8:

Since, just as the conventional usage of distinctions such as form and action is based on the cognition of distinctions like the space within a jar, so too the conventional usage of birth, death, and so forth is produced by the distinction between the body, the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*), and the individual soul (*jīva*); therefore, the impurity of the self consisting of the fruits of afflictions and karma is caused solely by that [distinction] and does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Desiring to establish this point through an illustration, he says:
Just as the sky appears soiled by impurities to the ignorant,
so too does the self appear soiled by impurities to those lacking wisdom.

Just as in the world the sky (*ākāśa*) appears soiled by thick dust, smoke, and other impurities to the undiscriminating fools, yet the sky does not become soiled for those who discern its true nature;

likewise, the Self (*ātman*), though supreme, appears as if defiled by the impurities of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and their fruits to the unawakened—those devoid of discrimination regarding the inner Self—and not to those who possess such discrimination.

The meaning is that the Self does not become defiled by the afflictions and other impurities superimposed upon it by the ignorant, any more than a desert region becomes possessed of water, foam, and waves merely because they are superimposed by living beings suffering from thirst. //8//
START MandUpK 3.9 He further elaborates on the very same point already stated: "In death and in birth, as well as in going and coming,"
In its abiding within all bodies, it is indistinguishable from space.

The meaning is that, like the birth, destruction, movement, arrival, and staying of the space within a jar, the birth, death, and so forth of the Self in all bodies are to be understood as non-different from [the nature of] space. //9//
All composite entities are like dreams, projected by the illusory power (māyā) of the Self;
for no logical justification exists for either their superiority or their total equality.
The aggregates such as the body, which correspond to the place of the jar and so forth, are emitted by the Māyā of the Self, like the body seen in a dream or like a body transformed by a magician;

the meaning is that they are presented by the Māyā-avidyā of the Self and do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). Whether there is an "excess" (*ādhikya*), meaning a state of superiority of the aggregates of effects and instruments such as gods in comparison to [lower] bodies, or whether all are equal—none of these is possible or established as having real existence.
The cause does not exist; for because [it does not exist], therefore they are produced by ignorance alone and do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality—this is the meaning. //10//
START MandUpK 3.11:
To demonstrate that the non-dual reality of the Self, which is devoid of origination and so forth, is established by the authority of scripture, the following passages are cited:
"Those sheaths beginning with 'rasa' which were explained in the Taittirīyaka..."
Their self, the supreme life-principle, has been clearly revealed as being like space.

The sheaths, such as that consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) and that consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), are explained—that is, clearly described—in the *Taittirīyaka*, specifically in the *Valli* of the *Taittirīyaka-śākhā-upaniṣad*. These are called "sheaths" because, like the sheath of a sword, each preceding one exists on the outside in relation to each succeeding one.
Their Self is that innermost Self by which all five sheaths possess a self-nature.
For he is called the *jīva* because he is the cause of life for all.
To the question "Who is he?", it is said: he is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who was previously introduced as "Brahman, which is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).

Since it has been stated that the aggregates characterized as the sheaths (kośas), beginning with *rasa* and proceeding through space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, are like dreams and illusions, emanated by the *māyā* of the Self;
that Self has been revealed by us to be just like space, through such verses as: "The Self is indeed like space" (Advaita 3).
The intention is that [the Self] is not accessible through the authority of human intellect as conceived by the logicians (tārkika). //11//
In each pair [of meditations], the Supreme Brahman is revealed through the knowledge of the honey:
on the earth and in the stomach, just as space is revealed.

Furthermore, the Person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality, who exists within the earth and so forth, both with respect to the divine and the internal self—the Knower, the Supreme Self, Brahman, who is all—is the Supreme Brahman revealed up to the exhaustion of duality in each pair [of elements]. To the question "Where?", he says: in that which is known as the Knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the honey, the nectar, the immortality; it is called the "Knowledge of Honey" (*madhujñāna*) because it is understood as the cause of delight, and thus refers to the Madhu Brāhmaṇa. In that [text], this meaning is established.
To the question "What is it like?", he says: "Just as in the world a single space is revealed by inference both in the earth and in the belly, so it is in this case"—this is the meaning. //12//

The non-difference between the individual self and the Supreme Self is praised through their identity; and that their difference is censured—this alone is indeed consistent with reason. (Mandūkya Upaniṣad Kārikā 3.13)

That the distinctness of the individual self (*jīva*) and the supreme Self (*para-ātman*), as determined through both reason and scripture, is praised and extolled by the sacred texts (*śāstra*) and by Vyāsa and others through their non-difference; and that the perception of manifoldness—which is common to all living beings, innate, and fabricated by sophists excluded from the scriptures—is censured [by such statements as]: "But there is no second thing besides it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23), and "From a second thing, indeed, fear arises" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.2).
2) "He makes a distinction within himself;
therefore, fear comes to him" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1);
"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6, 4.5.7).
7) By such statements as, "He goes from death to death who perceives here [in this world] as if there were multiplicity" (KaU 2.1.10), and by other authorities among the knowers of Brahman,
it is meant that this very [view] is consistent, straightforwardly intelligible, and logical.
The intention is that those false views imagined by logicians, when examined, are not straight and do not stand up to scrutiny. //13//

The distinctness between the individual self (jīva) and the Self (ātman) that was proclaimed prior to creation is figurative, based on a future state; for its primary sense is not tenable [at that time]. (MandUpK 3.14)

But is it not the case that even by Śruti, the distinctness of the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman) was proclaimed prior to their origination—that is, before the Upaniṣadic passages concerning origination—in numerous instances within the Karma-kāṇḍa according to the diversity of desires, such as "desiring this," "desiring that"? And the Supreme [Self] is said: "He supported the earth and the heaven" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.12).
1) By such scriptural passages as these mantras;
in that regard, how is the consistency of the meaning of the statements of the Jñānakāṇḍa—namely, unity alone—ascertained when there is a contradiction with the statements of the Karmakāṇḍa?
To this it is said: "From which indeed these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1).
1) “Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.10);
“From that very Self, indeed, space was produced” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.2);
“It thought” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).

3) That distinctness from [Brahman] which is proclaimed in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) prior to the Upaniṣadic statements concerning origination, such as "He emitted that heat" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), is not ultimate reality.
What then? It is figurative, like the distinction between the great ether and the ether within a jar.
Just as in the expression "he cooks rice," [the action is referred to] by way of its future occurrence;
for it is never possible for sentences concerning difference to have a primary meaning of actual difference,
because sentences concerning the difference of the Self merely restate the perception of difference among living beings caused by innate ignorance (*avidyā*).

And likewise, in the Upaniṣads, through statements concerning origination, dissolution, and so forth— such as “That thou art” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7–16) and “He who thinks ‘He is one and I am another’ does not know” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10)— it is precisely the oneness of the individual soul and the supreme self that is intended to be established.

Therefore, the intention is that since unity is what the Upaniṣads intend to establish through scripture, the reference to the perception of difference in the world is merely figurative, based on an anticipated state of affairs.
Alternatively, [it refers to passages such as] "It thought" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3) and "From that it emitted heat" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).
3) Prior to such origination, its oneness is proclaimed in the passage: "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.2).
And that very [oneness] is [referred to in] "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That art thou" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
8–16) Thus, with reference to that future state which will come to be, the distinctness between the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman) that is understood in certain passages is figurative;
it is just like the expression, "He cooks the rice. //14//

Objection: "But surely, although everything was before its origination unborn, one, and without a second, nevertheless, after origination, all this has been born and individual souls (jīvas) have become distinct.
Reply: Not so; for the scriptural texts concerning origination have a different purpose.

This objection has already been refuted previously: like a dream, these aggregates are projected by the self’s own *māyā*, and the birth and differentiation of individual souls (*jīva*) are like the birth and differentiation of the space within jars.

It is precisely from those scriptural passages concerning the birth and differentiation of souls that [the author] has drawn [this point], and now, with the desire to explain the true purport of the scriptural texts regarding birth, he presents them again:
"The creation which was taught otherwise, by means of clay, iron, sparks, and so forth..."
That is a means for entry; there is no difference whatsoever.

The various modes of creation that have been set forth and illuminated through the presentation of analogies such as sparks from a clay world and so forth— all those diverse ways of describing creation are merely means for us to lead toward the realization of the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self.

Just as in the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the narrative concerning the piercing by the evil of the Asuras involving speech and the other senses was fashioned for the purpose of leading to the understanding of the preeminence of the vital breath.
If it is argued that this too is unestablished, we say no; for in the various recensions (*śākhā*), dialogues concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are heard in different ways.
For if the dialogue were indeed the ultimate reality, the same dialogue would have been heard identically in all recensions; it would not have been heard in numerous contradictory forms.
However, it is heard [in scripture]; therefore, the concordant scriptures (*saṃvāda-śrutayaḥ*) do not have that [same] purpose.
Likewise, the originative statements (*utpatti-vākyāni*) are to be understood [as having a different purpose].

If it is argued that because of the differences between kalpas and creations, there is a variation in the concordant scriptures and the originative scriptures with each new creation (*pratisarga*), [we reply: no.
No; because it would be purposeless, as there is no purpose for the entry of cognition other than that which has already been stated.
Indeed, it is impossible to imagine that the scriptures concerning the arising of corroboration have any other purpose.
If it is argued that they exist for the sake of meditation in order to realize suchness, [we reply: no.

Because the arising, occurrence, and destruction of conflict are undesirable to realize, therefore the scriptural texts concerning origination and so forth are intended solely for the introduction to the realization of the oneness of the Self; it is not proper to assume any other purpose.
Consequently, there is no distinction whatsoever caused by origination and the like. (15)
START MandUpK 3.16:

If the Supreme Self alone—eternal, pure, awakened, and free by nature—is the one ultimate reality, as established by such scriptural passages as "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.2), then for what purpose has this meditation been taught, given that everything else is non-existent? [For instance: "The Self, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).
5) "The Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1, 3); "He should form a resolve" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1);
"One should meditate [on it] as the Self alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).
7) From such scriptural passages as these, [it may be argued that] ritual acts such as the Agnihotra and others [are required].
Listen to the reason for this:
The stages of life (āśramas) are of three kinds, characterized by inferior, middling, and superior views;
this instruction on worship was taught for their sake out of compassion.

This teaching on worship, as well as ritual actions for the sake of the stages of life (*āśrama*) and so forth, were taught by the compassionate Veda out of pity for those of dull or middling vision; they were not intended for those who have attained the supreme vision that the Self alone is non-dual. [The Veda asks: "How may the virtuous, walking upon the true path, attain this supreme vision of unity?
"That which the mind does not perceive, that by which they say the mind is perceived—"
"Know that alone to be Brahman, not this which people here worship" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.4);
"That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8–16); "The Self alone is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25).
3) From such scriptural passages as these. //16//
START MandUpK 3.17:
Because it is established through both scripture and reasoning, the vision of the non-dual Self is right vision; anything other than that is false vision because it stands outside of it.
Furthermore, the dualistic view is false vision because it is the locus for defects such as passion and aversion.
How so?
Those who maintain dualistic views are firmly convinced of their own established tenets;
they contradict one another, but this [non-dualist] is not contradicted by them.

Regarding their own established systems—the fixed rules for the composition of their respective doctrines—those who follow the views of Kapila, Kaṇāda, Buddha, the Arhats, and others are dualists and are firmly convinced that "this alone is the ultimate truth and not otherwise. Thus, being attached to this or that position and perceiving the opposing side as a threat to themselves, they hate it; in this way, possessed by passion and hatred, they conflict with one another solely on account of their adherence to their own philosophical systems.

This Vedic position of ours—the view that the Self is one because it is non-different from all—does not conflict with those mutually contradictory [views], just as [the body] does not conflict with its own hands, feet, and so forth.
The intended meaning is that the very cognition of the oneness of the Self, which is not a locus for defects such as attachment and aversion, is right vision (samyagdarśana). //17//
START MandUpK 3.18 It is stated by what reason they do not contradict [the scriptures]:
non-duality (advaita) is indeed the ultimate reality (paramārtha), while duality (dvaita) is said to be its differentiation.
For them, duality exists in both ways; therefore, this [teaching] is not contradicted by that.

For non-duality (*advaita*) is indeed the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); since there is no plurality, "diversity" refers to the differentiation of that non-duality, and the meaning is that it is the effect of that differentiation. [As stated in the scriptures: "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.2), and "That [Self] created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).

3) Thus, according to both scripture and logical reasoning, because [duality] is absent in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), in a swoon, and in deep sleep—states in which the vibration of one's own mind has ceased—it is called "duality" (*dvaita*) when there is a distinction between those states and that [absence].
For dualists, however, duality exists in both ways: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as well as from the perspective of non-ultimate reality (*aparamārtha*).
And if the dualistic view of those who are deluded is [false], whereas our non-dualistic view is the non-deluded one,
then for this reason, they do not contradict our position. "Indra, through his powers of illusion (*māyābhiḥ*), appears in many forms" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).
11) This is because of the Vedic scripture (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23): "But there is no second thing besides it.

Just as one mounted on an intoxicated elephant does not urge forward an insane person standing on the ground—even when that person says, "I am mounted on an elephant, drive the elephant toward me"—because he perceives no contradiction [between their states], in the same way, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the very Self of the knower of Brahman is [the Self] of those who perceive duality.
For this reason, our position is not contradicted by them. //28//
START MandUpK 3.19:
It might be suspected by someone that when it is said, "Duality is the distinction from non-duality," duality also must be ultimately real, just like non-duality; therefore, he says:
"For this [unborn] is divided by Māyā, and not otherwise in any way."
For if it were to be differentiated in reality, the immortal would indeed pass into mortality.

That non-dual reality which exists as the ultimate truth is indeed differentiated through *māyā*, like the many moons seen by those with ophthalmia, or like a rope appearing through various distinctions such as a snake or a stream; yet it is not so divided in the ultimate sense because the Self is partless (*niravayava*).
For that which has parts is divided by the alteration of its parts, just as clay is divided by the distinctions of jars and the like.
Therefore, the intention is that the partless and unborn [Brahman] is not divided in any way whatsoever by anyone.
For if it were divided in reality, the immortal, unborn, and non-dual [Brahman], being existent by its very nature, would fall into mortality—
just as fire [might fall] into coldness.
And that transition to a contrary nature is undesirable,
because it contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is unborn and undecaying, is differentiated only through illusion (*māyā*) and not in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, non-duality is not ultimately real. //19//
Proponents of [theories of] becoming desire the birth of an entity that is indeed unborn.
For how can an entity that is unborn and immortal undergo mortality?

Furthermore, those commentators on the Upaniṣads or proponents of the doctrine of Brahman who are eloquent speakers, yet desire that the very reality of the Self— which is unborn and immortal by nature— should have birth or origination even in the ultimate sense; for them, if it were born, it would necessarily fall into mortality.
And since that unborn entity is by its very nature immortal, how could it become mortal?
The meaning is that it can never attain mortality, as that would involve a contradiction of its own inherent nature. //20//
For this reason:
"The mortal does not become immortal, nor likewise does the immortal become mortal."
There can be no alteration of primordial nature (prakṛti) in any way whatsoever.
The immortal does not become mortal in this world, nor likewise does the mortal become immortal;
therefore, there can be no alteration of the inherent nature of primordial matter (prakṛti), nor any falling away from its own state by itself, just as heat cannot leave fire. //21//
If one's being, which is immortal by nature, undergoes mortality,
how can that which is made immortal by artificial means remain unshakable?

Furthermore, for that proponent who asserts that an entity which is by its own nature immortal attains mortality—that is, that it arises in the ultimate sense—how can his proposition that "prior to its arising, that entity is immortal by its own nature" be tenable? How can that entity, being produced, be immortal?
How will it remain stable as something of an immortal nature? It will not remain so at all, for one who maintains the doctrine of self-arising, there is simply no such thing as "birth" at any time.
All this is mortal;
therefore, the implication is that there would be no liberation. //22//
START MandUpK 3.23:
"But surely, for one who maintains the doctrine of non-origination (*ajātivādin*), the scripture that teaches creation lacks authority?
Certainly, there does exist scripture teaching creation."
But that [objection] is directed toward something else;
we have already stated that it is a skillful means for the purpose of introduction.

Now, even though the resolution has been given, these further objections and resolutions are intended solely to dispel any lingering suspicion regarding the conformity or contradiction of the literal words of the scriptural passages on creation with respect to the intended meaning.
Whether [the world] is created as real or even as unreal, the scriptural testimony is the same;
that which is certain and endowed with reason is [to be accepted], and nothing else. (MandU 3.23)

Regarding a thing being created as real from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the scriptural statement concerning creation is equal—that is, identical—to that concerning a thing being created through illusion (*māyā*) by an illusionist (*māyāvin*), which is not real.
Now, it may be argued that between a secondary (*gauṇa*) and a primary (*mukhya*) sense, it is logical for the word’s meaning to be understood in its primary sense.
This is not so; for we have already stated that otherwise, creation would be unestablished and purposeless.

Every creation, whether secondary or primary, is produced solely by ignorance and does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality, according to the Śruti: "For he is unborn, both within and without" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).
Therefore, we have stated in our previous writings that that alone—which is determined by the Śruti as the one, non-dual, unborn, and immortal—is consistent with reason and established by logic;
that alone constitutes the meaning of the Śruti, and nothing else ever can. //23//
How is the certainty of what has been heard established? To this he says:
"Because of the Vedic tradition that 'here there is no diversity,' and also because of [the verse] 'Indra by means of his powers of illusion'..."
Though unborn, he is born in many ways through his creative power (māyā).
For if creation were indeed real in its very essence, then the various things would truly exist, and consequently, there would be no sacred scripture intended to demonstrate their non-existence.
Yet, there exists such scripture as "There is not here any diversity whatsoever" (KaU 2.1.11), which serves the purpose of negating the existence of duality.
Therefore, the creation imagined for the purpose of realizing the oneness of the Self is indeed non-existent, like the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*);
for it is designated by the word *māyā*, which denotes a non-real object, in the passage: "Indra [acts] through *māyās*" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.19).
Is it not the case that the word *māyā* denotes wisdom (*prajñā*)?
True; however, there is no fault here because sensory wisdom (*indriya-prajñā*) is accepted as being *māyā* due to its being composed of defects.

The meaning is: "by means of *māyās*, that is, by means of sensory wisdoms which are of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*)," according to the Vedic revelation: "Though unborn, he is born in many ways."
Therefore, it is born through illusion alone;
the word "tu" (but/only) serves to emphasize—namely, "through illusion alone.
For it is not possible for both non-arising and manifold birth to coexist in a single entity.

Just as coldness and heat cannot coexist in fire, so too, because it possesses fruit, the vision of the oneness of the Self alone is the meaning determined by the Śruti, as seen from such Vedic verses as: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśopaniṣad 7).
And because the perception of distinctions such as creation and so forth is censured in the passage, "He goes from death to death" (KaU 2.1.10). //24//
By the denial of origination, origination itself is negated; by the question "Who indeed could produce this?", the cause is negated. (MandUkK 3.25)
"Into blind darkness enter those who worship the source of birth" (Īśopaniṣad 9);

by this negation of the worshipability of the source of birth (*saṃbhūti*), its very existence as such is prohibited. For a negation of that [source] is not logically tenable if it were truly existent in the ultimate sense.
Is it not the case that the negation of *saṃbhūti* (origination) has the purpose of enjoining a conjunction with *vināśa* (destruction), as in the passage:
“Those who worship ignorance enter into blind darkness” (Īśopaniṣad 9)?
True; the negation of *saṃbhūti* is indeed for the purpose of enjoining the conjunction of ritual action—denoted by the word *vināśa*—with the vision of the deity, which is the subject of *saṃbhūti*.
Nevertheless, it serves the purpose of crossing over death—which is characterized by destruction and consists in the activity of innate ignorance.

For in this way, a person who is freed from impurity in the form of the two-fold seeking (eṣaṇā) becomes consecrated (saṃskṛta). Therefore, ignorance (avidyā)—characterized by the combination of the vision of the deity and ritual action—is for the purpose of crossing over death.
Thus, for one who has crossed over death in the form of ignorance characterized by seeking, who is dispassionate, and who is intent on contemplating the meaning of the Upaniṣadic scriptures—
Since the arising of the knowledge of the oneness of the Supreme Self is not invariably concomitant [with ignorance], the later-arising knowledge of Brahman—

which is connected to the same person as the means for attaining immortality— is said to be "combined" with the earlier-arising ignorance. Therefore, because its purpose is different, the deprecation of *saṃbhūti* (becoming) serves only as a censure with respect to the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining immortality.
Even though it is the cause for the separation from impurity, it does not have that [impurity] as its ultimate basis.

For this very reason, because origination is denied, the existence of origination is merely relative; thus, with reference to the oneness of the Self which is real in the absolute sense (*paramārtha*), that origination called "immortality" is negated.

In this way, since the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is like a magical creation produced by ignorance—is established through ignorance, upon the destruction of ignorance it possesses its own essential nature; therefore, in the absolute sense, who indeed could produce it?
For no one can produce again a snake superimposed upon a rope through ignorance once it has been destroyed by discrimination;
likewise, no one could produce this [world]. Because the phrase "who indeed" (*ko nu*) has the sense of an objection, a cause is thereby denied.

The intention is that there is no causal agent whatsoever for that which has arisen from ignorance and has perished: "This was not born from anything, nor did anything ever come into being" (KaU 1.2.18).
Thus says the Śruti. //25//
This very [Self], because it negates everything explained as "not this, not this," shines forth as unborn by reason of its being ungraspable.

Considering the Self—taught by the negation of all specific attributes in the passage, “Now, therefore, the instruction: ‘Not this, not this’” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6)—to be difficult to comprehend, the Śruti repeatedly explains it through various other means with the desire to make that very Self known; yet [the opponent] rejects all that has been so explained and denies that which is graspable as an object of the intellect characterized by birth.
The meaning is this: by the statement “This is not this, not that” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26), the Śruti demonstrates the invisibility of the Self;

thus, for the sake of ensuring that what has been explained as a means—by one who does not know that the means culminates in the goal—does not become graspable like the goal itself, the Self is negated by way of its being ungraspable, which serves as the reason or cause.

And thus, for one who understands that the means (upāya) is directed solely toward the goal (upeya), and that the goal is of an eternally uniform nature, that reality of the Self—which is unborn and devoid of both exterior and interior—shines forth by itself. //26//

Thus, by hundreds of scriptural statements, it has been ascertained that the reality of the Self is unborn, without interior or exterior, non-dual, and that there is nothing other than this. Now, he says that this very point is further determined through reasoning: START MandUpK 3.27 Thus, by hundreds of scriptural statements, it has been ascertained that the reality of the Self is unborn, without interior or exterior, non-dual, and that there is nothing other than this.
Now, he says that this very point is further determined through reasoning:
For birth is possible through illusion, but not in reality;
for one who is born in reality, that which was already born would have to be born again.
In this regard, it might be argued that if the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) were always ungraspable, then it would simply be non-existent.
That is not so, because its effects are perceived;
just as the birth of a magician through his magic is an effect of that which exists.

Thus, the birth of the world, when perceived as an effect, leads one to understand that the Self—which is ultimately real like a magician—is the locus for the illusory manifestation of the world's birth.

For the birth of the world is logical only from an existent cause (*sat*), just as the production of effects such as elephants created by magic proceeds from a magician who exists; it does not proceed from a non-existent cause.
However, birth of the Self in an absolute sense is not logical.

Alternatively, just as the birth of an existing, real entity such as a rope occurs through illusion (*māyā*)— like that of a snake— and not in reality, so too the birth of the Self, which is likewise an existing reality though it is not an object of perception, occurs through illusion in the form of the world— like a snake in a rope— but not in reality; for there is no birth of the unborn Self.

Furthermore, for a proponent for whom the ultimately real, unborn reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) arises in the form of the world, it cannot be said that "the unborn is born," because of the contradiction.

Consequently, it follows by implication that "that which is already born is being born," and from that, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) results due to the continuous arising of what has already been born.
Therefore, it is established that the reality of the Self is one and unborn. //27//
The birth of that which is non-existent through illusion is not possible in reality;
a son of a barren woman is born neither in reality nor even through illusion. (MandUpK 3.28)

For proponents of non-existence (*asadvādin*), the birth of a non-existent entity is in no way tenable—whether through illusion (*māyā*) or in reality (*tattvataḥ*)—because it has never been observed.
Indeed, the son of a barren woman is not born either through illusion or in reality; therefore, the doctrine of non-existence is utterly untenable in this context. This is the meaning. //28//
START MandUpK 3.29 But how is it said that the birth of the existent occurs through illusion alone?—
just as in a dream the mind vibrates, appearing as a duality, through illusion.
In the same way, the mind vibrates through illusion, manifesting as the duality of the waking state.

Just as a snake imagined in a rope ceases to appear when it is viewed in its true form as a rope, so too the mind, when viewed in its true nature as ultimate cognition, ceases its vibration as the appearance of duality— the forms of the grasped and the grasper—
just as a snake [vanishes] from a rope in a dream or through illusion.
In that very same way, during the waking state, the mind vibrates through illusion; the meaning is that it appears to vibrate. //29//
The mind, though non-dual, appears as dual in a dream; of this there is no doubt. Likewise, it appears as dual in the waking state; of this there is no doubt. (MandUpK 3.30)
Just as a snake appears in the form of a rope, so too the mind—which in ultimate reality is non-dual in its nature as the Self—appears as dual; of this there is no doubt in a dream.
For in a dream, neither the objects of perception such as elephants nor the pair of sense organs such as the eyes that perceive them exist apart from consciousness.
The meaning is that it is exactly the same in the waking state as well.
Because there is no distinction in terms of being ultimate reality and being mere consciousness. //30//

START MandUpK 3.31 It has been stated that the mind itself, appearing in the form of dualistic conceptualization like a snake in a rope, is what constitutes duality. To this, he states an inference characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the proof for that claim.
How so?
This duality, whatever it may be, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is the visible manifestation of the mind;
for when the mind becomes non-mind, duality is no longer perceived at all. (MandUkK 3.31)
Therefore, since this entire duality of the visible world is conceptualized by the mind, it is the "mind-visible"; the proposition is that all this is the mind alone.
This is because [the visible] exists when that [mind] exists, and does not exist when that [mind] is absent.

For when the mind has become non-mind—having been dissolved like a snake in a rope through the cessation [of mental activity] achieved by the practice of discriminative insight and dispassion, or as in deep sleep—duality is no longer perceived; thus, its non-existence is established.
The meaning is that duality is non-existent. //31//
START MandUpK 3.32 But how does the state of being without mental constructs (amanībhāva) come about? It is said:
When, through the realization of the truth of the Self (ātmasatyānubodha), one no longer forms volitional constructs (saṃkalpayate), [then one is without mental constructs].
Then it attains the state of non-mind, for in the absence of an object to be grasped, there is no grasping of that [mind].
The Self alone is reality; it is the reality of the Self, just like clay. According to the Śruti, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4).
The realization following the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher regarding that [Self] is the "realization of the reality of the Self.
By means of that, because of the absence of any object of volition, one does not form any volitional constructs.
Just as there is no burning in the absence of fuel for fire, at whatever time—that is, at that very time—it attains "mindlessness," the state of being without mind;
in the absence of an object of perception, that mind becomes "non-grasping," meaning it is devoid of the conceptualization of grasping. //32//
START MandUpK 3.33:
If this duality is non-existent, by what means is one's own unborn reality of the Self awakened? To this it is said:
They declare that knowledge is non-conceptual, unborn, and non-different from the object of knowledge.
The unborn, eternal Brahman, which is to be known, is realized by the unborn as the unborn.

The knowers of Brahman declare that knowledge—which is non-conceptual, free from all conceptual construction, and for that very reason unborn, consisting of pure consciousness (*jñapti-mātra*)—is non-different from Brahman, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sat*), which is the object of knowledge.

For it is said: "There is no loss of the knower's power of knowing, just as heat is never absent from fire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30); "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28);
and "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).
This is established by such scriptural passages as these.

Its specific qualification is "Brahman is to be known" (*brahma-jñeya*), which means that this Brahman to be known is non-different from its own self, just as heat is non-different from fire. By means of that unborn knowledge which is one's own essential nature, one awakens to and realizes the unborn reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) by oneself alone.
The meaning is that, like the sun whose nature is eternal light, [the Self], because it is a solid mass consisting solely of eternal consciousness, does not require any other knowledge. //33//

It has been stated that by the realization of the truth of the Self (*ātmasatyānubodha*), one who no longer forms volitional constructs (*saṅkalpa*) becomes one whose mind is pacified, restrained, and suppressed— like a fire without fuel— in the absence of external objects. And thus, it has also been stated that when the mind attains the state of non-mind (*amanībhāva*), there is the absence of duality (*dvaitābhāva*).
The movement of that very mind, when thus restrained, non-conceptual, and possessed of wisdom, should be understood as being like that in deep sleep; it is not otherwise equal to that.

The movement of the mind that has been restrained, ceased, free from conceptualization, devoid of all mental constructions, wise, and discerning—that movement indeed must be specifically understood by yogis.

Now, one might object: "If there is an absence of all cognitions, then the movement of the restrained mind would be exactly like that of the mind in deep sleep, since there is no difference in the absence of cognition; what, then, is there to be known therein?
To this it is said: It is not so.

Because in deep sleep there is one state of activity for the mind— which is seized by the darkness of the delusion of ignorance and possesses the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are the seeds for the manifold activities of unwholesome states—

and quite another, independent state of activity for it when all the dust of afflictions has been stilled, once the seeds for the activities of ignorance and unwholesomeness have been consumed by the fire of the realization of the Truth of the Self and the mind has been restrained.
Therefore, he is not equal to that;
thus, it is logical that he is capable of knowing—this is the intended meaning. //34//
He states the reason for the difference in their conduct:
"For it dissolves in deep sleep; that which is restrained does not dissolve."
That very Brahman is fearless, the light of knowledge extending everywhere.

For in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), the mind dissolves (*līyate*) along with all the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the seeds of notions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, attaining a state of being a seed that is of the nature of darkness (*tamas*) and undifferentiated.

However, when [the mind] is restrained and suppressed through the prior realization of discrimination (*viveka-vijñāna*), it does not dissolve; it does not attain the state of being a seed of darkness. Therefore, the difference in the mode of activity between the mind in deep sleep and the mind in meditative absorption (*samāhita*) is logical.

Just as when it is freed from the two stains produced by ignorance— the grasped and the grasper— then that very thing becomes the supreme non-dual Brahman; therefore, that alone is fearless Brahman, peaceful and without fear, because the apprehension of duality, which is the cause of fear, has ceased to exist, so that the knower does not fear anything whatsoever.

That very [Brahman] is further qualified: *jñapti* is knowledge, which is consciousness (*caitanya*) as the essential nature of the Self; that very knowledge is the light (*āloka*), the illumination, of which that Brahman is possessed—this is the meaning of "the light of knowledge" (*jñānāloka*). It means that Brahman is a solid mass consisting of the single flavor of pure consciousness (*vijñānaikarasaghana*). "On all sides" (*samantataḥ*) means everywhere, pervading without interruption like space (*vyoma*). //35//
Unborn, without Indra, sleepless, nameless, and formless; shining once for all, the omniscient—of this, no figurative description can be made in any way whatsoever. (MandUkK 3.36)
Because of the absence of any cause for birth, it is unborn both internally and externally;
for we have stated that birth is caused by ignorance, like [the appearance of] a snake in a rope.
And since that ignorance has been ceased through the realization of the truth of the Self, it is therefore unborn and, for that very reason, sleepless.
Ignorance is beginningless illusion, characterized as sleep;
because one awakens from that sleep by means of the Self whose nature is non-dual, it is therefore "without sleep. For its name and form exist only due to the absence of awakening.

And because of its awakening, it is as if destroyed like a snake [perceived] in a rope; thus it is not designated by name, nor is Brahman described by any means whatsoever, and so it is "nameless and formless.
This is according to such scriptural passages as: "From which words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1).

Furthermore, it is "shining once" (sakṛdvibhātam) because it is always shining; it is eternally of the nature of light (bhārūpa), being devoid of the appearance and disappearance of non-apprehension and erroneous apprehension.
For night and day—characterized by apprehension and non-apprehension—and darkness, which is the mark of ignorance (avidyā), are the causes for the lack of constant shining.
Since those are absent and because its nature is eternal consciousness and light, it is logical that it is "shining once."

Therefore, because it is both everything and the very nature of the Knower, it is "all-knowing" (sarvajña). In this case, with respect to Brahman, no such figurative application (upacara) or metaphorical designation should be made,
as is done for others who are distinct from their own essential nature through designations such as "concentration" (samādhi) and so forth.

Since Brahman has the nature of being eternally pure, enlightened, and free, there is no possibility whatsoever—by any means at all—of anything to be accomplished; the meaning is that this refers to the destruction of ignorance. //36//
START MandUpK 3.37 He states the reason for the establishment of the aforementioned meaning by virtue of its being nameless: "It is devoid of all verbal expression and has arisen beyond all thought."
It is supremely tranquil, a single light, an unshakable and fearless meditative absorption.
"Expression" (*abhilāpa*) is that by which something is expressed; it is the instrument of speech (*vāk-karaṇa*) for all modes of designation.
He is "devoid" (*vigata*) of that.
Here, "speech" (*vāk*) is used as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); the meaning is that he is free from all instruments of conceptual construction (*brahma-karaṇa*).

Likewise, it is "arisen from all thought" (*sarvacintāsamutthita*). Thought (*cintā*) is that by which something is thought; it is the intellect (*buddhi*). "Arisen from that" means it is devoid of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), according to such scriptural passages as: "For he is without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 2.1.2).
Because it is devoid of all objects, it is therefore perfectly tranquil;
it is ever-luminous, being eternally light by virtue of its nature as the self's consciousness;
and it is samādhi, because it is to be realized through the wisdom that takes samādhi as its object.
Alternatively, it is called *samādhi* because one becomes concentrated (*samādhīyate*) therein;
it is immovable and changeless, and for that very reason it is fearless, due to the absence of modification. //37//
START MandUpK 3.38 Since Brahman alone is said to be the unshakable and fearless samādhi— wherein there is neither grasping nor rejection, and wherein no thought exists—
Then that knowledge, established in the self, becomes unborn and attains equanimity.
In that Brahman, there is no grasping—that is, no seizing or taking up—nor is there any casting off—that is, no relinquishing or abandoning.
For where there is modification or the state of being an object thereof, there might be abandonment and acquisition; but those two do not exist here in Brahman.
Because there is no other cause for modification and because it is partless, there is neither rejection nor acquisition therein; this is the meaning.
It is that wherein no thought exists.
The meaning is that where, due to the state of being mindless (*amanastva*), no thought whatsoever is possible, how could there be rejection or acquisition?
At the very moment the realization of the truth of the Self arises, knowledge—which is established in the Self alone because of the absence of objects—abides in the Self itself like the heat of fire;
it is unborn (*ajāti*) and devoid of birth.
It has reached equanimity; it has attained supreme equality.

That which was initially promised—"therefore I shall speak of non-miserliness, which is unborn and has reached equanimity"—is here concluded both through logical reasoning and scriptural authority as "the unborn has reached equanimity."

Apart from this realization of the truth of the Self, everything else falls within the domain of wretchedness, according to the Śruti: "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is indeed wretched" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.10).
The intended meaning is that having attained this, every Brāhmaṇa becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. //38//
START MandUpK 3.39 Even though this is the ultimate reality in this way—
the yoga known as "the Untouchable" (asparśayoga) is indeed difficult to perceive for all yogis—
For yogins fear this [Self], seeing fear where there is no fear.
This is called the "untouchable yoga" (*asparśayoga*) because it is devoid of all contact known as "bondage"; indeed, it is traditionally remembered as such in the Upaniṣads.
It is "difficult to perceive" (*durdarśa*), meaning it is difficult for all yogins who lack the knowledge prescribed by the Vedānta—by all such yogins;
the meaning is that it can be attained only through the effort of realizing the truth of the Self.

For yogis indeed fear this [Self], even though it is free from all fear; they feel dread because they regard this yoga as the destruction of the self. They perceive fear in this which is fearless; the meaning is that these undiscriminating ones have a habit of perceiving the destruction of the self as the cause of fear. //39//
But for those for whom the mind, the senses, and so forth exist only as imagined— like a snake in a rope— and do not exist in reality apart from the nature of Brahman,
there is, by their very nature, fearlessness, liberation, and imperishable peace, which is the nature of Brahman itself.
Thus we have stated that [this state] is established as independent of anything else and is not a mere metaphorical designation in any way whatsoever.

However, for those other practitioners on the path who possess inferior or middling views and perceive the mind as something distinct from the self and related to it—for them, being devoid of the realization of the truth of the self, fearlessness depends upon the restraint of the mind; this applies to all yogins.
The destruction of suffering, awakening, and indeed imperishable peace.
Fearlessness for all yogins depends upon the restraint of the mind;
moreover, there is even the destruction of suffering [dependent on it],
for indeed, for those lacking discrimination, there is no destruction of suffering as long as the mind connected with the self remains agitated.
Furthermore, even self-awakening is dependent solely upon the restraint of the mind;
likewise, even that imperishable peace called liberation is dependent solely upon the restraint of the mind. //40//
Just as the overflowing of the ocean might be checked by a single drop with the tip of a blade of kusha grass,
so too the restraint of the mind may be achieved through tireless effort.

The meaning is that even the restraint of the mind for those who possess perseverance— provided their internal organs do not falter and they are free from despondency and exhaustion— occurs like the undertaking of drying up the ocean by scooping out a single drop with the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Is the mere possession of undaunted perseverance the only means for restraining the mind?
"No," it is said:
"One should restrain the mind when it is distracted by sensual enjoyments, and likewise when it is overly tranquil or in a state of lethargy; as is desire, so is lethargy. (MandUk 3.42)

Possessing undaunted perseverance, he should restrain—that is, control—the mind that is distracted by the objects of sensual enjoyment by means of the method to be described hereafter, so that it remains within the Self alone.

Furthermore, "laya" (dissolution) refers to deep sleep, as one dissolves into it; in that state of dissolution, he should restrain the mind so that it is "well-pleased," meaning free from exhaustion, and also "withdrawn"—the word "restrain" is understood to carry over from the previous sentence.
If it is already well-composed, why is it said to be restrained?
It is because, just as desire is a cause of misfortune, so too is lethargy (laya).
Therefore, the meaning is that the mind must be restrained from lethargy just as it is from the objects of desire. //42//
What is that means? It is said: having recollected that all is suffering, one should turn away from the enjoyment of desires.
Having recollected that all is the unborn, one does not see anything born at all.

Having recollected that all duality is a manifestation of ignorance and is nothing but suffering, one should turn back the mind—which has been scattered toward the enjoyment of desires, that is, objects of longing caused by desire—by means of the cultivation of dispassion; this is the meaning.

Having recollected through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher that the unborn Brahman is everything, one no longer perceives the collection of dualities which is its opposite, because of their non-existence. //43//

One should awaken the mind when it is dormant, and again pacify it when it is distracted; one should recognize it as being affected by impurities, and once it has attained equanimity, one should not disturb it. (MandUpK 3.44)

Thus, by this twofold means of the practice of knowledge and dispassion, one should awaken the mind when it is dissolved in deep sleep and unite it with the vision of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self.
"Citta" and "manas" are not different in meaning;
and when the mind is distracted among the enjoyments of desire, one should again pacify it.

Furthermore, as one practices again and again, one should recognize that the mind— which has been awakened from lethargy and turned away from sense objects, yet has not attained equanimity and remains in an intermediate state— is accompanied by impurity, possessed of passion, and conjoined with the seeds [of affliction]. Therefore,
one should strive with effort to bring it to a state of equanimity.

But when it has attained equilibrium—that is, when it is tending toward the attainment of equilibrium—one should not cause it to waver; that is to say, one should not allow it to turn toward sense objects. //44//
One should not relish pleasure therein; being free from attachment, one should become established through wisdom.
One should strive to unify the mind that is moving outward so that it becomes motionless. (MandUkK 3.45)
The meaning is that the yogi who is intent on meditative concentration should not savor the bliss that arises, nor should he become attached to it.
How, then, should he act?

Free from attachment and free from desire, one should contemplate through wisdom—that is, through the intellect of discernment—that whatever pleasure is perceived is merely false, being conceptually constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
The meaning is that one should thereby restrain even the craving for such pleasure.

Furthermore, when the mind—which has turned away from the craving for pleasure and possesses a steady nature—is about to go out, issuing forth externally, one should, by means of the aforementioned method, diligently restrain it from here and there and unify it within the self alone.
The meaning is that one should bring about the mere existence of the very nature of the mind. //45//
When the mind does not dissolve nor is it distracted again, being unwavering and free from appearances, then that is the perfected Brahman. (MandUkK 3.46)

When the mind, restrained by the aforementioned means, does not sink into deep sleep nor is it distracted again by sense objects— remaining unwavering, immovable, like a lamp in a windless place, and non-manifesting, meaning it does not appear as any object imagined through conceptual construction— then [it has attained its true state].
When the mind possesses such characteristics, then Brahman is perfected; the meaning is that the mind becomes perfected in the very nature of Brahman. //46//
They declare that supreme bliss to be self-abiding, tranquil, characterized by liberation, ineffable, unborn,
and known through the unborn object of knowledge; it is omniscient.
As it has been said: the ultimate happiness, characterized by the realization of the truth of the self, is established in its own state, abiding within itself;
it is peaceful, consisting in the cessation of all misfortunes;
and it is accompanied by Nirvana—that is, it exists together with Nirvana, which is liberation and absolute isolation.
And that is inexpressible, for it cannot be described;
because its object is absolutely unique,
that supreme, unsurpassed bliss is indeed the direct perception of the yogi alone.
"Just as 'unborn' (*aja*) refers to that which has not been born, so too [the term] refers to the object of experience.

The knowers of Brahman declare that bliss is none other than Brahman itself—the omniscient one—which, being non-different from the unborn, unarisen object of knowledge, exists in its own nature as the form of the all-knowing. (47)
START MandUpK 3.48:

All this, beginning with the restraint of the mind, is a creation like that of clay, metal, and so forth; and meditation has been taught as a means for attaining the realization of the ultimate reality, not as something ultimately real.
But the ultimate reality is...
No living being is born; its origination does not exist.
This is that supreme truth wherein nothing whatsoever is born.
No living being (*jīva*) is born; no agent or enjoyer arises in any manner whatsoever.
Therefore, for this single Self (*ātman*), which is by nature unborn, there exists no origin—that is, no cause.
Since its cause does not exist, it follows that no living being is born.
Among the truths previously described as means, this is the supreme truth: that in Brahman, whose very nature is truth, not even an atom of anything whatsoever is born. //48//
